video_title: Lawfare Daily: Gulf Countries Hedging Amid Iran War Debacle
gist: Two Middle East analysts argue the Gulf monarchies are hedging as the eight-month US-Iran war damages them, with Iran hitting even mediators, a possible UAE side deal with Iran, and Saudi diversification of security. They see a tactical pause, depleted US munitions, little help from China or Russia, and a hard path to a deal after the midterms.

themes.theme: Gulf hedging strategy and the protection paradox

insights.claim: GCC states are hedging like investors in a risky market with three layers: keep working with the US, act more independently (diplomacy, regional security, restraining the US), and in select cases accommodate Iran.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Gulf alignment is becoming multi-vector, so US-centric regional assumptions (basing, arms, investment) deserve a discount.

insights.claim: US-led integrated air and missile defense still failed to fully protect the Gulf: CENTCOM cited >500 ballistic missiles and 6,000 attack drones intercepted in the initial combat phase, yet missiles got through, US bases were hit, and interceptor inventories were strained.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Interceptor depletion is a durable demand driver for air defense and a vulnerability for the security guarantee.

insights.claim: Gulf infrastructure risk was existential: strikes on desalination plants threatened urban water supply and in May drones launched from Iraq hit close to the UAE's lone nuclear power plant.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Tail-risk pricing of Gulf critical infrastructure (water, nuclear, energy) is warranted.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait were reported to have conducted covert retaliatory air strikes inside Iran while publicly denying offensive roles.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Gulf states are more willing combatants than public posture suggests, which raises escalation risk.

insights.claim: The administration did not plan for a war lasting more than a couple of weeks or for the effect of a long war on regional allies; the GCC likely told Washington to have a plan, be fast and be decisive, and it was not.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Planning failure is the root of the credibility loss with allies.
insights.quote: for God's sake, have a plan, make it fast, and make it decisive

themes.theme: Gulf-US rift and Saudi security diversification

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia, which wanted a NATO-style treaty, has brought in 8,000 Pakistani troops, launched a 13-partner maritime alliance for Red Sea shipping and the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement; these are nascent hedges that cannot yet replace US guarantees but could become consequential if the US keeps falling short.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Watch Saudi-Pakistani defense ties and Red Sea coalitions as a signal of structural alignment drift.

insights.claim: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman led GCC appeals that contributed to Trump calling off additional strikes when he threatened dramatic escalation including civilian infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: The Gulf holds a de facto brake on US escalation, via appeals and potentially denying airspace and basing.

insights.claim: Riyadh asked Washington to intervene militarily as the Houthis seized territory near Bab el-Mandeb and attacked Saudi Arabia; the administration declined while securing Houthi assurances not to threaten US shipping, which did not sit well with Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: US-Saudi trust erosion and persistent Red Sea shipping risk.

insights.claim: Threatening Oman with bombing while it mediates and is struck by missiles is poor alliance management; Oman's coexistence policy with Iran is geography-driven and non-negotiable.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: US coercion of mediators reduces diplomatic off-ramps and pushes Gulf accommodation of Iran.

themes.theme: Iran's targeting logic and escalation options

insights.claim: Iran cannot strike the US homeland, so its doctrine is to raise US costs by hitting the US footprint in the region, and Gulf states are prime targets because their value proposition is stability and wealth (energy, tourism, business); striking airports and energy aims to make them press Washington to stop.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: Iranian pressure on Gulf aviation, energy and tourism assets is a deliberate lever, not collateral.

insights.claim: All GCC states were struck in this war, even mediators Qatar and Oman; Ari reads the strikes on mediators as more reflex than strategy, and notes the Iranian system is poorly understood after months of change.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: Opaque Iranian decision-making reduces forecast reliability for any ceasefire call.

insights.claim: The UAE was hit harder than any other GCC state early on (including Fujairah oil infrastructure in early May), then Iran apparently did not strike UAE territory in July and August even while retaliating elsewhere; a Reuters report said the UAE agreed to pay Iran up to $20 billion, though payment is unconfirmed.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Possible bilateral Gulf side deals with Iran would fragment the GCC position and signal cheaper security via accommodation.
insights.quote: Iran did not strike UAE territory once during that period for the whole month of July and August

insights.claim: Expect Iranian horizontal escalation if the war resumes: cyber attacks on US critical infrastructure, threatened drones on a US bomber base in the UK, and terrorism against Jewish community centers and Europe-based US-linked bases.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: Raises cyber and soft-target risk premia outside the Gulf.

insights.claim: The current lull in Iranian fire on Gulf states (3+ weeks) is a tactical pause, not strategic, in a pause-strike-pause-strike cycle; Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are actually rising and Iran is threatening retaliation as the US weighs sending more carriers.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: Do not read calm as de-escalation; the risk of renewed strikes is live.

insights.claim: A major US bombing resumption in November is doubtful because the war badly depleted key US munitions that take years to replace, which has caused internal administration debate.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: Munitions constraint caps US escalation capacity and supports defense replenishment demand.
insights.quote: I'm not entirely convinced we're going to see a major resumption of bombing campaign in November

insights.claim: Both Iran regime collapse and regime survival are bad for the GCC: collapse risks an Iraq or Syria-style security vacuum the administration has not considered.
insights.speaker: Shawn Howard (ex-CIA)
insights.so_what: No clean positive endpoint, so a long volatility regime is the base case.

themes.theme: China, Russia and the deal outlook

insights.claim: China and Russia have little interest in ending the war: it distracts the US, drains munitions, diverts US carriers from the Indo-Pacific (China), strains NATO and reduces Ukraine bandwidth (Russia); China may at most help with nuclear implementation such as taking Iran's enriched uranium.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: No external mediator will rescue a settlement; the war's drag on US resources benefits rivals.

insights.claim: A deal is hard because the June memorandum front-loaded concessions that no prior administration would give, so anything less will be rejected; Iran also sees the US as an unreliable partner after the JCPOA withdrawal.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: The negotiating anchor is set too high for a quick deal; the post-midterm talks may change little.

insights.claim: Iran can sustain the murky state because the regime points to the war to defer governance failures and protests that have worsened; prewar status quo was better for the US than any post-war outcome, which favors Iranian patience.
insights.speaker: Ari (Chicago Council)
insights.so_what: Time favors Iran's consolidation while US costs (munitions, gas and grocery prices, domestic division) rise.
